sections.panorama:
Overview: why Antalya is different

The day's highlights, with links to the sources, are in Today at COP31.

When9–20 November 2026
WhereAntalya EXPO Fairgrounds, Aksu, Türkiye
PresidencyTürkiye, Murat Kurumhost country, Action Agenda, communications
NegotiationsAustralia, Chris Bowenagenda, core texts, Pacific voice
Three tests (E3G)
  1. Credible response to the science and the 1.5 °C overshoot
  2. Finance reaches those who need it most
  3. The Paris regime moves into the implementation era
2035 NDCs~150 Partiesthree quarters of emissions; a third of the cut needed
Pre-COPFiji, Tuvalu and Palau

COP31 takes place from 9 to 20 November 2026 at the Antalya EXPO Fairgrounds (Aksu, Antalya, Türkiye), and will be judged by one question: can implementation of the Paris Agreement become measurable and financeable without losing the 1.5 °C goal? Belém set the political mandate; Antalya must turn it into investment, infrastructure and verifiable results.

Three features make this COP unprecedented:

  • Split co-presidency. Türkiye holds the official Presidency (Murat Kurum, Minister of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change), and manages the venue, the Action Agenda and communications. Australia, through Chris Bowen, is the "President of the Negotiations": he leads the negotiating agenda, drafts the core texts and represents the interests of the Pacific islands. Under the modalities agreed in November 2025, nothing moves without the approval of Ankara and Canberra.
  • Adverse geopolitical context. War, an energy crisis (the Hormuz shock), an emerging El Niño and the highest FAO food price index since 2022. E3G argues that the response to this volatility and to the climate transition is the same: clean electrification, grids and resilience.
  • Overshoot assumed. UNEP projects that the "lowest possible overshoot" scenario takes warming to 1.7–1.8 °C in the mid-century before returning to 1.5 °C by 2100. For the first time, Parties are negotiating on the basis that exceeding 1.5 °C is likely.

Türkiye comes to the role of host with ambiguous credentials: a Climate Law in force since July 2025, a neutrality target for 2053, an ETS regulated in August 2026 and 79.4 GW of renewable capacity (11th in the world), but also Europe's largest coal generation fleet (34% of electricity in 2025, with state purchase guarantees until 2029) and an NDC 3.0 (643 MtCO₂e in 2035, about 40% above 2018 levels) rated "critically insufficient" by the Climate Action Tracker. The pre-COP was held in Fiji, Tuvalu and Palau, as part of an agreement between the two countries.
sections.belem:
From Belém to Antalya: what was settled and what was left open

Belém advanced the implementation agenda but left delivery to Antalya. The practical rule for reading any announcement: distinguish adopted decisions (negotiated, binding), political signals (decision text without a number or operational deadline) and presidency initiatives (voluntary, outside the negotiated process).

Topic What Belém delivered What was left open for Antalya
Finance Two-year Climate Finance Work Programme (CFWP) on Article 9; guidance to the GCF, GEF and FRLD; Baku–Belém Roadmap to US$1.3 tn US$1.3 tn is a mobilisation ambition, not cash; composition and contributor base of the NCQG stalled; report by the Brazilian presidency on the roadmap
Adaptation 59 Belém Adaptation Indicators (BAIs); political signal to triple adaptation finance by 2035; Belém–Addis Vision (B2A) through to COP32 Link between the GGA and finance (collapsed in Bonn under Rule 16); indicators task force; the value of "tripling" (LDCs ask for US$120 bn/year)
Just transition Agreement to develop the Belém–Antalya Mechanism (BAM) under the JTWP Governance, finance and scope of the BAM; review of the JTWP
Fossil fuels No negotiated phase-out language survived, despite more than 80 countries supporting it; TAFF roadmap led by the presidency (not negotiated) How the TAFF connects to the cover text and the electrification initiative; future of the process after COP31
Forests Deforestation roadmap (zero and reverse by 2030) and launch of the TFFF Country and biome milestones, finance trajectories and the scale of the TFFF
Trade First explicit mention of unilateral trade measures; reaffirmation of Article 3.5 of the Convention; annual dialogues in Bonn (2026–28) and the Integrated Forum (IFCCT) No trade dialogue at COP31; the topic is expected to resurface in just transition and response measures
Implementation Global Implementation Accelerator (GIA) and Belém Mission to 1.5 (BM1.5), run by a coalition of presidencies (COP29–31) Presidencies' reporting on the GIA; whether the initiatives add value or fragment the architecture further
Information integrity First decision to recognise climate disinformation Operationalisation

On NDCs, only about 150 Parties (three quarters of global emissions) have submitted plans for 2035; Iran, Viet Nam, Egypt and Argentina still have no new NDC, and the United States has withdrawn its own. Even with full implementation, current NDCs would deliver only a third of the cut needed for the lowest-overshoot scenario (UNEP, Emissions Gap Report 2026).

The shift in focus is visible: Belém prioritised nature, tropical forests and South–South solidarity; the Turkish–Australian presidency is organising the Action Agenda around electrification, zero waste, resilient cities and green industrialisation, keeping the transition away from fossil fuels out of the spotlight.
sections.testes:
The three tests for COP31

E3G proposes assessing Antalya not by a single result, but by three tests that together show whether the package connects ambition to delivery.

1

Credible response to the science and the 1.5 °C overshoot

Mitigation must limit the scale and duration of the overshoot; adaptation must protect those already suffering locked-in impacts; loss and damage must reach those already paying the price. Signals to watch: an energy package that treats methane, clean power, electrification and structural transition as mutually reinforcing (IRENA notes that 35% electrification by 2035 requires a 48% fall in the fossil share); a continuing process for the TAFF roadmap that feeds into the GST2; a baseline and trajectory for tripling adaptation finance (which fell from US$28 bn in 2022 to US$26 bn in 2023); new pledges to the FRLD (only US$822 million pledged, about half paid) and support for Nepal's recovery after the glacial floods in August (minimum losses of US$2.69 bn); progress on the deforestation roadmap and the TFFF; and a "Blue COP" with a clear political signal on oceans.

2

Finance reaches those who need it most

In 2024 developed countries provided and mobilised US$136.7 bn, but that figure predates the aid cuts; ODA is expected to fall a further 6.9% in 2026, and the GEF replenishment came in 27% below the previous cycle. Welcome signals: new or renewed multi-year pledges; clarity on the grant and concessional share; a plan to triple adaptation; a 2027 work plan for the CFWP that addresses provision, access and quality together; more countries outside Annex II reporting voluntary contributions (WRI estimates US$102 bn of South–South cooperation between 2013 and 2023); endorsements of Australia's Finance Access Declaration; MDB commitments on the cost of capital (local-currency lending, simpler guarantees, transparency on default data); and country platforms that reach financial close.

3

The Paris regime moves into the implementation era

With the rulebook complete and consensus under pressure, the question is whether the process strengthens delivery, transparency and accountability. E3G describes a two-tier model consolidated in Belém: the institutional tier (negotiations, universal rules, financial architecture) provides legitimacy; the implementation tier (coalitions, presidency roadmaps, sectoral alliances, the Action Agenda) demonstrates that ambition is achievable. In practice: a closing plenary for the Action Agenda that consolidates the year's progress under the six pillars; ministerial pairs per pillar towards the GST2; a focus on making the existing system work rather than launching new initiatives; defence of the IPCC and the scientific base (the AR7 timetable and budget need to be resolved at the resumed IPCC-65); trade dialogues with a clear mandate and technical support from the WTO and UNCTAD; recognition of ISDS as a barrier to transition; and green industrialisation treated as an implementation opportunity.

E3G's synthesis for those going to Antalya: support the presidency with firm defence of the science, a tangible finance offer (access and mobilisation), early ambition expectations for the GST2, continuity of the TAFF and the electrification pledge, and solidarity with Nepal.

sections.radar:
Pre-COP radar (Climate Home News, 5 November)

  • Cover decision. Australia admits referencing the 1.5 °C overshoot, the electrification goal, methane, early warning, access to finance and nature-based solutions (forests and oceans). Two open questions: whether or not to include the TAFF roadmap (Europe and the islands in favour, fossil producers against) and whether to make explicit that electrification relies on clean energy (EU position).
  • Agenda fights before the plenary. The African Group asked for three new items, including adaptation finance and trade (to link the Bonn dialogues to formal negotiation within two years, with European resistance expected). Nepal wants a work programme on mountains and climate after the August flood. China wants to address trade measures that restrict clean technology equipment. Bowen needs to resolve this before 9 November.
  • Adaptation. Belém's tripling has no base year, value, modality or payers; in Bonn the Europeans refused to insert it into the GGA text. The Adaptation Gap Report estimates that tripling would reach US$85–120 bn/year against US$305 bn of needs. The EU arrives without new pledges; the Adaptation Fund and the new Pacific Resilience Facility will ask for contributions.
  • Just transition mechanism. Australia treats it as the main deliverable. LMDCs and the Arab Group oppose using it to push the TAFF; Latin Americans and islands want the TAFF and tripling renewables to advance; developed countries demand that it not create new financial obligations. CAN proposes a "resource mobilisation group" under the mechanism.
  • MWP. LDCs and islands want a stronger mandate tied to the GST; Saudi Arabia, India and China are expected to oppose.
  • GST2 and IPCC. A majority wants the AR7 reports ready for the GST2 (conclusion in November 2028); Saudi Arabia, India and Russia resist, arguing it would harm scientists from developing countries. The last IPCC meeting was suspended after the sixth failure to agree the timetable; an extraordinary online meeting is scheduled for early December. An option under discussion: the cover decision asking for timely IPCC inputs, with leaders brokering.
  • Electrification. The pledge (to be launched on Energy Day, 10 November, with a list of signatories) does not require clean energy: it refers to "diverse and sustainable sources" according to national circumstances. Electricity currently accounts for 23–24% of final consumption; the Climate Action Tracker projects only 28% by 2035 under current policies. Australia in, Europeans likely, India expected to refuse, China undecided.
  • Green industrialisation. A Green Industrialisation Facilitation Mechanism will help LDCs turn industrial plans into projects (it is not finance); the Global Green Industrialization Agenda, hosted by UNIDO, builds on the Belém declaration endorsed by 19 countries.
  • Oceans. Türkiye is preparing a declaration; the coalition of more than 100 countries (Brazil, the EU, African countries) wants an implementation plan, not just recognition. The Arab Group opposes discussing a fossil transition in the ocean negotiations; Ilana Seid (AOSIS) calls the TAFF "the best way" to ease pressure on the ocean.
  • Forests. The Turkish Action Agenda has practically dropped deforestation; the Brazilian roadmap remains the reference, with implementation the responsibility of countries.
  • Tensions. Türkiye states that it has the final word on the outcomes; divergence between the co-presidencies over progress is a mapped risk. Investigation points to Koç Holding, a major sponsor, with a refinery at full capacity and climate targets being scaled back. Participants were warned not to interfere in Turkish "internal affairs"; authorisation for Saturday's march was still pending. The Africa Energy Bank was launched on 3 November, mainly focused on oil and gas.
sections.thinktanks:
What think tanks and networks say

What think tanks and networks say (survey of 6 November)

Survey of 25 institutions in the UNFCCC space (full report separate). The consensus is that Antalya will not produce a major negotiated result and will be judged by architecture, not ambition: the disputes are over institutional form in each track. What matters is where they diverge.

Topic Convergence Divergence or new data
Electrification 35 by 35 Target works as a floor; CAT: current policies give 28% in 2035, Paris-aligned pathways require 34–41% (54–68% by 2050) Only open divergence in the North: WRI (Nick Wayth) says "clean power should not be a prerequisite"; Germanwatch, CAT, Wuppertal and Greenpeace (a 75% renewable floor by 2035) demand anchoring in renewables. WBCSD wants electrification in the text without a condition. CAT rates Türkiye "critically insufficient", with electrification stalled at ~21% since 2013 and an official projection of 25% in 2035
Co-presidency Implementation as a criterion ODI (Colenbrander): "an awkward alliance"; two-thirds of the electricity of the two countries is still fossil. Germanwatch: Australia "noticeably absent" at the pre-COP. IDDRI more generous (Türkiye as a North–South bridge)
Finance No one expects substantive progress; an agenda fight over item 9.1 is likely Germanwatch: Baku–Belém roadmap with "little political traction"; WRI expects "more detail". South–South rift: the AGN asks for an agenda item on tripling adaptation, while LDC negotiators (Raju Pandit Chhetri, Nepal) consider it unworkable and call adaptation a "homeless issue"; SIDS lean toward the developed countries on the broad focus (access, donor base). The US$ 120 bn target appears as 2030 or 2035 depending on the source
Just transition mechanism CAN: functions and modalities in Antalya plus a transitional committee to operate until COP32 Three camps in the South: the AGN wants a CMA body along the lines of the SCF ("non-negotiable"); the LMDC wants a "cooperation network" with no new obligations; AOSIS wants a technical arm. The Pacific and AILAC want the TAFF to advance; the LMDC and the Arab Group reject any fossil-fuel conditionality
Loss and damage Permanent agenda item and replenishment through levies on polluters Only Germanwatch puts a number on it: US$ 50 bn in the 2027 replenishment, rising to ~US$ 400 bn by 2035. Nepal: the FRLD Board set aside US$ 20 mn on 22 October ("symbolic", according to Nepalese officials) against a US$ 4.7 bn need
TAFF and GST2 IDDRI, Carbon Brief and Germanwatch: do not reopen the negotiated text; look for a procedural hook that takes the roadmap to the GST2 Germanwatch calls on Brazil for its deforestation roadmap. IDDRI proposes six dimensions for national submissions to the GST2. IPCC-65 failed for the sixth time to agree the AR7 timetable and did not approve a budget; the trust fund runs out in 2028; an extraordinary meeting in December is not confirmed
Host Monitor, don't boycott Global Witness: TPAO gas output rising from 8.2 to 22 bcm by 2035; Koç has cut its 2030 targets (27% to 20%) and Tüpraş its 2035 targets (35% to 25%). Urgewald: >€2.4 bn a year in coal subsidies. Amnesty: more than 100 detained in the September operation, more than 1,000 accounts blocked

Notable gap: no Brazilian think tank (Observatório do Clima, Talanoa, iCS) has published analysis dated October–November on COP31, and no one has assessed the Climate Implementation Bridge beyond one-line descriptions. Interpretation of Brazil's roadmaps in Antalya is likely to come from IDDRI and Carbon Brief

Full report, survey of 6 November 2026

Think tanks call for implementation, not promises, in Antalya

Think tanks, civil society networks, and finance and science institutions that follow the UNFCCC converge on a diagnosis: COP31 (Antalya, 9–20 November 2026) will not produce a major negotiated outcome and should be judged by three tests. The first is whether the "35 by 35" electrification goal becomes a trackable package anchored in renewables. The second is whether a delivery pathway emerges for the US$ 300 bn NCQG and for tripling adaptation finance. The third is whether the Just Transition Mechanism (JTM/BAM) gains functions, governance and a transitional committee that makes it operational by COP32 in Addis Ababa. The real disagreements are few but important. WRI says "clean power should not be a prerequisite to increasing electrification", while Germanwatch, Climate Action Tracker, Wuppertal and Greenpeace (which sets a 75% renewables floor for 2035) argue that without a fossil-fuel condition the goal becomes a "Trojan horse". The African Group wants a CMA body for the JTM that is "non-negotiable" and an adaptation agenda item, while the LDC Group considers the item unworkable and the LMDC wants a "cooperation network" without obligations. The South uses OECD figures (US$ 136.7 bn in 2024, 67% in loans, 7% for low-income countries) as proof of non-delivery, not of compliance. The starkest numbers are in loss and damage (the FRLD has received US$ 486 mn against US$ 2.8 bn requested) and in science (IPCC-65 failed for the sixth time to agree the AR7 timetable and did not even approve the budget). IDDRI, Carbon Brief and Germanwatch treat the Brazilian roadmaps on transition away from fossil fuels and forests (3 November) as a useful, voluntary input whose value depends on a procedural hook at COP31 that takes them to the GST2. The largest analytical gap is Brazilian and Southern: no publication from October–November 2026 on COP31 was found from the Observatório do Clima, Talanoa, iCS, Power Shift Africa, CEEW, CAN International, ITUC or WWF

The success criterion has shifted from negotiated text to "what countries will do differently"

All Northern institutions start from the premise that Antalya is an "implementation COP" without an emblematic decision. WRI writes that COP31 "is not expected to produce a landmark negotiated outcome", and Ani Dasgupta sums up the test: "COP31 shouldn't be judged by new pledges alone, but by what countries agree to do differently" (WRI). IDDRI (Marta Torres Gunfaus, 5 Nov) asks whether the conference can "accelerate action on the ground" and calls electrification "the central political test", adding that "a target alone will not deliver this transformation" (IDDRI). What differentiates the institutions is how prescriptive they are about the formal text. The German ones are the most demanding: Germanwatch published on 3 November the only explicit scorecard, with three criteria. These are "Visible implementation of the Paris Agreement", "Strengthening the UNFCCC process" (an Action Agenda with "clear responsibilities, timelines, and monitoring", the design of the GST2, and "signal willingness to evolve the UNFCCC") and "Mobilising adequate finance". It proposes "a group of willing states to pioneer reform if full consensus is not possible" (Germanwatch; COP31 hub). The Wuppertal Institut (Fischedick and Obergassel, 5 Nov) wants the 35% target "anchor[ed]" in the formal outcomes and warns that the transition away from fossil fuels has "increasingly been pushed into the background" (Wuppertal). WRI and IDDRI, by contrast, accept that the main result will come from the Action Agenda and political signals, a difference of emphasis rather than of position

The newest and least consensual point is the assessment of the co-presidency. ODI (Sarah Colenbrander) calls the Australia–Türkiye pairing "an awkward alliance", notes that more than two-thirds of both countries' electricity still comes from fossil fuels (against 35% in Latin America and under 30% in the EU), and makes success conditional on "the host countries quickly agreeing a shared vision" with a clear chain of command (ODI). Germanwatch describes Australia as "noticeably absent" before the COP (p. 13), while IDDRI is more generous, seeing Türkiye as a "North-South bridge-builder" and Australia as guaranteeing the voice of the Pacific (Germanwatch PDF; IDDRI). Carbon Brief adds the most relevant operational information for anyone navigating the COP: the Australian presidency is "intending" to seek a "cover text" that could capture goals such as electrification (Carbon Brief)

In the South, the framing is identical but the subject is different: delivery by developed countries. AGN Chair Antwi-Boasiako Amoah said in Nairobi that "Antalya (Turkey) must be about delivery, not another cycle of promises" and that Africa "was not asking for charity" (Ghana News Agency). PICAN, already in Antalya on 6 November, states that "We cannot afford a COP that lowers ambition when the science demands greater urgency" (PICAN). Among Chinese analysts, Kate Logan (ASPI) predicts that "China's top priority at COP31 will be upholding multilateralism" and that Beijing will be "happy to let other developing countries push this agenda while serving as a broker in the end game" on finance (Carbon Brief). Vice-Minister Li Gao called on COP31 to "facilitate in-depth discussions on a roadmap for developed countries to deliver the $300 billion climate finance goal by 2035" (Global Times). India (Bhupender Yadav, 3 Nov) wants the GST to be "Party-driven, facilitative and non-punitive" (News On AIR), a sign that any cover decision comparing NDCs with 1.5 °C trajectories without equity language will be contested

The Hormuz crisis entered every analysis as a tailwind for the electrification narrative, not as an excuse for delay. Germanwatch gives the harshest numbers: about 20% of world oil trade interrupted, "the most severe energy disruption since the 1970s" (p. 7), and the US withdrawal from the Paris Agreement left "a significant hole" in financing that other developed countries "should not use this as an excuse to reduce ambition" (Germanwatch PDF). WRI notes that "the war on Iran has raised oil and gas prices" and that a possible Super El Niño could push 50 million people into acute hunger (WRI). No Northern think tank models quantitatively the effect of the American exit or ODA cuts on the trajectory of the US$ 300 bn, and CSIS, the most likely to cover the US and Hormuz, has published nothing on COP31

"35 by 35" electrification: the only explicit disagreement is whether it must be clean

The presidency's goal, raising electricity's share of final energy demand to 35% by 2035, is the most analysed initiative and the one generating the only open disagreement among institutions. Nick Wayth (WRI) states that "clean power should not be a prerequisite to increasing electrification". WRI calls on countries to sign the pledge and publish roadmaps covering supply, demand, grids, storage and tariffs, recalling that emerging economies received only 15% of global clean energy investment in 2024 (WRI). On the other side, Germanwatch demands "anchor '35 by 35' in renewable energy", and researcher Kerstin Opfer writes that "countries could increase electricity consumption while continuing to rely on fossil-fuel power" and that "The goal must be renewable-based electrification" (Germanwatch blog). The Climate Action Tracker (Climate Analytics + NewClimate, 2 Nov) provides the technical basis: current policies lead to only 28% in 2035, the goal requires accelerating electrification "almost four-fold", Paris-compatible pathways reach 34–41% in 2035 and 54–68% in 2050, and "35% should be seen as a floor for ambition rather than a ceiling". Samuel Guéret warns that "electrification only limits overshoot if the electricity is cleanly generated" and that "taken alone, countries could meet the target by simply adding electricity to the system", for example through data centres (CAT; briefing). Greenpeace is the most specific: the goal is only meaningful with "scaling renewable power generation to at least 75% by 2035" (IEA NZE: 77%), coal exit in developed countries by 2030 and gas exit by 2035, and rejection of nuclear, CCS, biomass and gas as a "transition fuel" (Greenpeace briefing COP31; electrification briefing). The WBCSD, the only business coalition with a document in the period (30 Oct), wants "electrification outcomes included in the COP outcome" and a clean-energy segment at the Leaders' Summit, but does not impose a clean-energy condition (WBCSD). Yao Zhe (Greenpeace East Asia) predicts that China "likely remains reluctant to link these targets to any commitments regarding transitioning away from fossil fuels" (Carbon Brief). In other words, the fight in Antalya will be over whether electrification language carries any fossil-fuel qualifier

Anyone citing the goal should pay attention to the baseline discrepancy. IDDRI and Germanwatch say "just over 20% today"; WRI, "23% today"; CAT and Carbon Brief, "almost 24% in 2023". The IEA, in its special report of 22 September, uses ~23% and calculates that exploiting all currently cost-competitive potential would take it to ~33%, which places the 35% above business as usual but within reach (WRI on IEA). The IEA estimates the goal requires demand growth of ~1,400 TWh a year (almost double the decade's average), grids expanding 40% faster, battery storage multiplied tenfold to ~2,900 GW, and that importers could save ~US$ 400 bn a year in fuel (Down to Earth). President Kurum argues that "The level was not chosen politically" and that renewables and electrification are "the surest and cleanest way to protect citizens around the world from high and volatile energy prices" (Carbon Brief)

Turkish analysts accept the framing and use the COP to force a domestic decision on coal, while international NGOs attack the design of the goal. Ümit Şahin (IPC/Sabancı) argues that "a complete coal phase-out by 2036 appears technically and economically feasible" (Daily Sabah). The İklim Ağı hopes that "COP31 [will] be the one where Türkiye decides to phase out coal" (Daily Sabah), and Ember calculates that Türkiye could electrify 85% of final energy use with existing technologies (Anadolu). But CAT classifies Türkiye as "Critically insufficient", with electrification flat at ~21% since 2013 and an official projection of only 25% in 2035, below the target the country itself proposes to the world. It also records that in 2024 Türkiye overtook Germany as Europe's largest coal generator (CAT). Urgewald lists planned coal expansions of 688 MW (Afşin-Elbistan A) and 1,050 MW (Cenal, Çanakkale) and >€2.4 bn a year in subsidies. Heffa Schücking: "Electrification without phasing out coal is like showering with polluted water" (Eco-Business). Claire Smith (Beyond Fossil Fuels): "Let's not let electrification become the Trojan horse of our times" (Euronews). Germanwatch is the only one to connect electrification to the circularity of critical materials, and to propose using the 2028 GST to set post-2035 targets (Germanwatch blog)

Finance: the fight is over the agenda (Article 9.1, adaptation) and over how to read the OECD numbers

No institution expects substantive financial progress. IDDRI rates a breakthrough as "highly unlikely" and describes the presidency's Access to Finance Declaration as "lacking teeth" (IDDRI). Germanwatch says the NCQG still lacks an implementation plan, that the Baku-to-Belém Roadmap has "little political traction" and "assigns neither responsibility nor accountability measures", and that the Veredas Dialogue (Art. 2.1c) produced "an exchange of positions without measurable progress" (pp. 22–24). It therefore "expects an agenda fight unless Presidencies engage" on the finance work programme, and calls on the SCF to separate provision (9.1) from mobilization (9.3) and to define "new and additional" (Germanwatch PDF). This reading contrasts with WRI's, which neutrally expects the COP29 and COP30 presidencies to bring "more detail" on the roadmap and a monitoring system to Antalya (WRI). Política por Inteiro's January analysis already noted that the roadmap was only "taken note of" in paragraph 47 of the Mutirão, that negotiators "had often not read it, and no Party championed it", and that its relationship to the report of the Circle of Finance Ministers "was unclear" (Política por Inteiro). The Xingu Finance Talks in Bangkok (11 and 13 October) had a presence "skewed toward civil society and a few MDBs, with fewer Parties than expected", and no source confirms publication of the first expert group report promised for October (Down to Earth).

October's substantive novelty is the letter from Ghana, which chairs the AGN, to Simon Stiell asking for three additional agenda items: tripling adaptation finance, trade and climate change, and GCF financing arrangements (with no needs assessment since COP19). Amoah writes that "a dedicated item is needed" and that the Belém agreement "omitted the baseline year, a headline amount, who should pay, and how delivery would work" (Climate Home News). Here the first South–South fissure appears: Raju Pandit Chhetri, chief finance negotiator for the LDCs, considers a standalone item difficult to obtain and calls adaptation "a homeless issue" that must be discussed in some formal forum. No other group had endorsed the African proposal as of 28 October, and Mattias Söderberg (DanChurchAid) predicts it "may lead to an agenda fight" (Climate Home News). The LDC Dili Ministerial Declaration (3 September) calls for "at least USD 120 billion well in advance of 2035" and a finance programme focused "especially article 9.1" (tralac). The target year for the USD 120 billion figure is contested even within the same organizations: Greenpeace's briefing uses "$120 billion by 2030", while its 4 November release says "at least USD 120 billion a year by 2035" (Greenpeace). Política por Inteiro reads the paragraph 53 baseline as 2025 (~USD 40 billion), which makes tripling by 2035 worth ~USD 120 billion, "less than half of the US$300 billion NCQG goal" (Política por Inteiro). Germanwatch argues that tripling requires "a trajectory, timeline, baseline, and accountability framework" and is achievable "even if the overall climate finance does not increase" (p. 19). A second fissure: according to Carbon Brief, small island states line up with developed countries in favour of a broader focus (access, donor base), against the G77/LMDC insistence on 9.1 (Carbon Brief).

The data both sides will bring to the room are in the table below. The dispute is not about the numbers but about what they measure: developed countries will cite the OECD (third year above USD 100 billion) and the multilateral development banks ("on track" for 2030); developing countries will point to the share of loans, the 7% for low-income countries and Oxfam's real-value discount. Sehr Raheja (CSE) on the two-year lag in OECD data: "It undermines trust. A two-year delay is significant" (Down to Earth).

The debate on the cost of capital and debt has moved to the G20, the IMF and the World Bank and is expected to be only "noted" in Antalya. In Bangkok, the Bridgetown Initiative summed up that countries "cannot swap [their] way to survival" (a swap with a 60% guarantee yielded 6% interest; 80% would have yielded 4.5%), and Rishikesh Ram Bhandary (BU GDP Center) said the instruments under discussion are "not designed to unlock meaningful fiscal space over the long-term" (Down to Earth). Greenpeace and Amnesty converge on taxing polluters as a source: Greenpeace asks for a workstream in the finance programme on "progressive environmental taxation at national, regional and global levels" through the UN tax convention (Greenpeace); the Loss and Damage Collaboration states that developed countries could mobilize "6.6 trillion USD annually" (L&DC). Trade is the third front: Malaysia puts the CBAM among its priorities ("you cannot use climate change as a trade barrier") and records a fall in GEF transfers from USD 36 million to USD 13 million (The Star). The AGN and Russia have floated a formal negotiating track, and China "has signalled it wants COP31 to address trade 'protectionism'" (Climate Home News). IDDRI expects the CBAM to "feature prominently" and trade to be "one of the more contentious issues" (IDDRI). On Article 6, the only live item is the 5% share of Article 6.4 proceeds for the Adaptation Fund, which Germanwatch sees as "a predictable revenue base" (Germanwatch PDF).

Just Transition Mechanism: a CMA body or a facilitative network, with or without a fossil-fuel condition

The JTM (Belém–Antalya Mechanism, "BAM") is the item where civil society most clearly defines an "ambitious outcome", and the bloc positions mapped in Bonn show why it will be difficult. Anabella Rosemberg (CAN International) defines the ambitious result as setting out the functions and modalities in Antalya "with a transitional committee to make it fully operational by COP32 in Ethiopia in 2027", plus a "resource mobilisation taskforce" (Climate Home News). Germanwatch calls for clear governance, dedicated capacity and finance from rich countries, and notes that the mapping of initiatives mandated in Belém is incomplete (pp. 15–17); WRI suggests "a just transition technical support hub"; Wuppertal notes that developed countries are reluctant to offer concrete financial support (Germanwatch PDF; WRI; Wuppertal). Amnesty calls to "Fund and make accountable the Just Transition Mechanism", with Indigenous peoples and workers involved in decisions (Amnesty).

The institutional design splits the South into three camps. The African Group wants "a fully constituted CMA body" modelled on the SCF, which it called "non-negotiable", rejects a dialogue platform and wants finance assessed by "additionality, grant-equivalence, non-debt creating"; the LMDC (via Saudi Arabia) wants a "facilitative, demand-driven cooperation network" that does not create "new standards, benchmarks, or reporting obligations"; AOSIS backs a technical expert arm; AILAC wants the mechanism under the CMA as the main venue; India "cannot accept any renegotiation" of the mapping as a precondition (TWN Bonn Update No. 5). The second axis is scope: rich countries prefer a narrow focus on fossil fuels, while developing countries want a "whole of economy, whole of society" scope with green industrialization. The LMDC and the Arab Group want to avoid "targets, requirements, or conditionalities on transitioning away from fossil fuels (TAFF)", while "some Latin American and small island states" want the JTM to advance TAFF and the tripling of renewables; the EU rejects using the mechanism to contest the CBAM (Climate Home News). The inference is that the fight in Antalya will be about institutional weight (body versus network) more than about a fund, whose creation the United Kingdom has already said it has no mandate to support.

Trade unions have no document of their own in the period (nothing from the ITUC in October–November), but the African trade union front is the most articulated: the AGN and unions (ITUC-Africa, IndustriALL, NLC, Ghana TUC) agreed in Accra on a liaison group before COP31 and a common position rejecting loans as climate contributions, demanding local processing of lithium and cobalt, opposing the CBAM and linking ILO standards to finance. Paule-France Ndessomin (IndustriALL): "For African trade unions, the just energy transition is a fight against new green extractivism" (Ghana News Agency). In South Africa, Maesela Kekana concedes: "On adaptation, we don't really know where we are" (Daily Maverick). On the mitigation work programme, Germanwatch wants its continuation "without making its continuation contingent" on finance or fossil-fuel disputes (p. 17), and the LDCs call for a permanent and strengthened mandate (tralac). Carbon Brief records that the item was pushed to COP31 under rule 16 without agreed text (Carbon Brief).

Loss and damage: USD 486 million in cash against USD 2.8 billion in requests

The loss and damage fund arrives at Antalya with the most quantified "pledged versus needed" gap on the agenda. The Fund Board's report to COP31/CMA8 records pledges of USD 822.71 million as of 31 July 2026, USD 485.97 million received, the approvable envelope under the Barbados Implementation Modalities raised to USD 342 million, 176 conforming requests from 119 countries totalling USD 2.8 billion, LDCs and SIDS accounting for 60.8% of the requested value, and no approvals yet. An "initial starter package" goes to the December B.10 meeting (UNFCCC FCCC/CP/2026/7). The figures circulate in different versions that should be kept apart: "available" appears as USD 342 million or USD 350 million; "pledged" as USD 822 million or "less than US$1 billion"; "received" as "less than US$500 million" (Greenpeace). Nepal's case has become the test of the fund's rapid-response function: the Board's first extraordinary meeting, on 22 October, provisionally voted to reserve USD 20 million for recovery from the August glacier collapse (1,455 dead; needs of ~USD 4.7 billion), 45 days after the request by developing-country members. Nepalese authorities called the sum "symbolic", the World Bank offered an additional USD 170 million loan 28 days after the disaster, and Nepal has taken on more than USD 6 in loans for every USD 1 in grants over the last decade (Climate Home News; Kathmandu Post/ANN). Fill the Fund carries the demand into COP: "Speed must be built in, not improvised" (Climate Home News).

Demands converge on a permanent agenda item on loss and damage (Greenpeace; Germanwatch, which links it to the implementation of Article 8) and on replenishment through levies on polluters, but only Germanwatch puts a figure on it: US$ 50 bn a year in the 2027 replenishment, rising to ~US$ 400 bn in 2035, against needs of US$ 447–894 bn a year in 2030, and it records that Germany is "rather hesitant" (pp. 20–21) (Germanwatch PDF). L&DC, CAN and Fill the Fund did not publish a numerical replenishment target in October–November. PICAN adds a qualitative demand that goes beyond money: "recognition that some losses cannot be monetised", and its peaceful demands include reparations for non-economic losses and rejection of CCS and geoengineering (PICAN; PINA).

GST2, IPCC and Brazil's roadmaps: the procedural hook is the realistic prize

The convergent landing zone among IDDRI, Carbon Brief/IISD and Germanwatch on the fossil fuel transition is procedural: not a new negotiated TAFF target, but a hook at COP31 that routes the global roadmap and national roadmaps into GST2 as inputs. Germanwatch warns that reopening formal TAFF negotiation risks "another divisive debate" and prefers the Action Agenda and the national roadmaps from Santa Marta (p. 14), while demanding that "Brazil must deliver a roadmap to halt and reverse deforestation by 2030" (p. 13) (Germanwatch PDF). IDDRI (Van Rossum and Torres Gunfaus, 5 Nov) describes the COP30 Presidency roadmap, published on 3 November, based on 268 submissions, with three dimensions, a "Belém Readiness Approach" index and a proposed "TAFF Mutirão" by 2033, as "a useful contribution", whose main risk is limited impact "in the absence of a follow-up process agreed at COP31" (IDDRI). The IDDRI issue brief is the most operational contribution: it proposes six dimensions for national submissions to GST2 (technical constraints, finance, macro-fiscal dependence, employment, governance, participation), which can be packaged into national roadmaps or LT-LEDS, and states that "The COP30 Presidency Global TAFF Roadmap provides a valuable basis for organizing this evidence" (IDDRI brief). Carbon Brief (Daisy Dunne) records the roadmap's own recommendation that "COP31 should formally recognise the global roadmap and create a route for its findings to inform the second global stocktake", the 85-to-84 division in favour of versus against the reference in Belém (the list of opponents is inconsistent), and the observation that some countries see the focus on electrification as a way to avoid reopening the COP30 debates (Carbon Brief). Greenpeace Brasil (Carolina Pasquali) called the roadmap "a crucial step" that "stops short of setting clear fossil fuel phase-out targets" (Greenpeace). The Pacific sets the red line opposite to LMDC's: COP28 language "should not be reopened" (The Diplomatic Insight), while the Gulf bets on a "realidad de doble vía" and the Saudi minister called the net zero scenario "un la la land" (EFE/Revista Mercado). On the Brazilian side, Marina Silva framed the roadmaps as "Não é impositivo, mas é um caminho que nós não podemos deixar por menos" (O Liberal/Estadão); no Brazilian think tank published analysis dated October–November on the roadmap or COP31.

GST2 begins in Antalya with little political attention and a scientific input problem. IDDRI notes that the information-gathering phase "has received little political attention" and that evidence must arrive before June 2027 (IDDRI). IPCC-65 (Addis Ababa, 12–16 October) was the sixth consecutive session to miss the AR7 timetable and also failed to approve the 2026–27 budget; Jim Skea suspended the meeting, calling it "profound disappointment"; India, Kenya, Russia and Saudi Arabia want later publication (the India/Saudi option: WG2 in April 2029, WG3 in July 2029), China opposes more than three plenaries a year and says the reports need not be linked to the stocktake, and the trust fund will be "depleted by the end of 2028" at current contribution levels, with the US not having contributed since 2024 (Carbon Brief). The LDCs call for "all three IPCC AR7 Working Group reports completed in 2028" (tralac); Germanwatch says "political disagreement must not undermine the scientific process" (p. 9). No document proposes specific decision text for COP31 on the IPCC–GST2 link, and the December extraordinary session has not been confirmed. The blocking coalition (Saudi Arabia, India, Russia, China) is the same as in the finance and mitigation debates, which suggests linkage in Antalya. In the scientific background, the Emissions Gap Report 2026 estimates emissions of ~58.4 GtCO2e in 2025, flat, with cuts of 18% by 2030 and 45% by 2035 needed for the lower-overshoot pathway, while NDCs deliver 5–8% and 11–15% (Vajiram & Ravi); UNEP's "Limiting Overshoot" report already treated the 1.5 °C excess as "now unavoidable" (IUCN). Germanwatch turns this into a criterion: any overshoot must remain "short and shallow" (Germanwatch).

On adaptation, the newest framing is Germanwatch's: adaptation must be "a key political deliverable on a par with mitigation" (p. 19), with a pragmatic taskforce mandate agreed early, disaggregated indicators and preparation for Addis Ababa (Germanwatch PDF). Carbon Brief notes that the 59 GGA indicators must be refined by COP32, and that in Bonn the reference to tripling was left in square brackets, with Canada, Norway and Japan opposed, and a dispute between an "expert-driven" taskforce (Brazil, EU) and a "party-driven" one (Grupo Sur, LMDC, Arab Group) (Carbon Brief Bonn). WRI proposes "common resilience metrics" and investment by insurers and banks in resilience (WRI).

Action Agenda, sponsorship and civic space: host credibility as a red line

On the presidency's initiatives, the dominant criticism is one of accountability. Germanwatch demands that the Action Agenda have "clear responsibilities and timelines, continuity across Presidencies, and regular public monitoring" to avoid greenwashing, and asks for clarity on the mandate of the Green Industrialisation Accelerator (pp. 12, 17) (Germanwatch PDF). WBCSD offers the most detailed institutional design: an "Action Agenda delivery package", Blue Zone access tied to progress reporting, and an Action Agenda segment in the closing plenary with "Axis Pairs" reporting aggregate progress (WBCSD). The Climate Implementation Bridge, the presidency's proposal to turn NDCs into an "investable project portfolio" and correct fragmented pipelines, receives only one-line descriptions (Carbon Brief, UNU-EHS, Down to Earth on Bangkok); no think tank has assessed it and Germanwatch does not mention it (Carbon Brief; UNU-EHS). This is a significant gap for anyone tracking the design of the initiative.

For the host's credibility, the civil society red line is specific, and the numbers are new. Global Witness (19 October, Rystad data) shows that TPAO's gas output is set to nearly triple from 8.2 to 22 bcm by 2035, that the company plans more than 1.1 billion barrels of undeveloped assets by 2050, with at least 11 agreements with BP, Shell and Chevron since the COP bid, and that Woodside will double LNG by 2032 and Santos will multiply oil production eightfold by 2035 (Global Witness). Koç Holding, a COP31 "Global Business Partner", cut its 2030 targets in 2025 from 27% to 20% below 2017, and Tüpraş cut its 2035 target from 35% to 25%, with Scope 3 (~97% of the footprint) carrying no target; Pascoe Sabido (Corporate Europe Observatory) says the "climate integrity" check in the host agreement "doesn't appear to be worth the paper it's written on" (Climate Home News). There is no joint letter on sponsorship; the criticism is carried by individual organisations and investigative media, not by a coordinated action along the lines of "Kick Big Polluters Out".

On civic space, networks are adopting a posture of documented monitoring, not boycott. Amnesty records more than 100 people detained in the September operation against LGBTI+ organisations, more than 1,000 accounts blocked (including Amnesty Türkiye's) and the takeover of an opposition TV channel in October, and concludes: "No puede haber justicia climática si no hay libertad para exigirla" (Amnesty). AFP records 4,412 detentions before the NATO summit in July; Özlem Katışöz (CAN Turkey): "We are not expecting the government to treat COP like Nato", and Bengisu Özenç (SEFiA) says Turkish civil society's influence has been "quite limited" for lack of a formal consultation process (Malay Mail/AFP). The Peoples' Climate Summit (Halkların İklim Zirvesi) has "over 300 organisations from 100 countries" committed and a march on 14 November, but dates vary between sources (from 9 November according to AFP; 14–18 according to bianet) (bianet). The broader letter to the presidency remains the June letter from 94 Turkish and Australian organisations, sent in Bonn, asking Kurum and Bowen to act as an "honest broker" and to operationalise the JTM with finance and deadlines (Greenpeace Australia Pacific).

Beyond the missing institutions, three themes lack analysis: no one has assessed the Climate Implementation Bridge beyond one-line descriptions; no one has quantified the share of renewables needed alongside "35 by 35" beyond Greenpeace's floor; and no think tank has modelled the effect of the US exit and ODA cuts on the trajectory towards the US$ 300 bn for COP31 specifically.

Conclusion

What emerges from the notes is not a debate about ambition but about architecture: each track in Antalya has an institutional-form dispute built in — body vs. network on the JTM, agenda item vs. "homeless issue" on adaptation, a target anchored in text vs. the Action Agenda on electrification, a procedural hook vs. a new TAFF target, and three calendar options for the IPCC. For those navigating the COP, this means wins and losses will be read in procedural paragraphs (a transitional committee, a reference to the roadmap in the GST2 text, a taskforce mandate, an IPCC extraordinary meeting), and that the Australian cover text is the only place where electrification could gain a fossil qualifier — the issue on which WRI, alone among the institutions, prefers not to press.

The second implication concerns who speaks. The analytical North is mobilised and detailed (Germanwatch, IDDRI, CAT, Greenpeace), the institutional South speaks mainly through negotiators and the press, and the Brazilian analytical voice is absent at the moment Brazil delivers its two roadmaps and hands over the presidency. This opens space — and creates risk — for the interpretation of the roadmaps in Antalya to be made by IDDRI and Carbon Brief, not by those who know them from the inside.

Update of 6 November: what the missing networks and think tanks add

A second sweep covered the institutions with no material located in the first pass (CAN, ITUC, WWF, Oxfam, DCJ, 350.org, Oil Change, NRDC, L&D Collaboration, Observatório do Clima, Política por Inteiro, ECCO, ENB, Power Shift Africa, CEEW, CSE, NewClimate, CSIS, ICC, WMB, Eurodad, V20/CVF, Arab Group, UNEP). Almost all published between 29 October and 6 November. What changes in the reading, track by track:

  • Finance and Art. 9.1. The agenda fight at the opening plenary has become a consensus reading (Eurodad, ENB, AGN, Arab Group, CSE). The Arab Group's submission calls for launching the 9.1 work programme "at COP31/CMA8", with an agenda item through CMA10 and "without shifting the financial burden to developing countries"; the EU Council (9 Oct) responds that "broadening the base of contributors is a necessity". Kurum, in the UNFCCC preview (5 Nov), sided with the South: "We do not need new targets. We need to deliver on the ones we have, with developed countries taking the lead."
  • Adaptation. A numerical floor has taken shape from civil society for tripling: at least US$ 120 bn a year "well before 2035" (CAN-I, Oxfam, NRDC, CSE, AGN), based on 2025 levels; WWF reads the target as "6x 2019". The Adaptation Gap Report 2026 (need of US$ 305 bn a year by 2035; flows of around US$ 30 bn in 2024) is the figure everyone cites; CAN and Germanwatch demand that tripling gain a trajectory, a baseline and sources rather than being parked in the finance room. The Adaptation Task Force bulletin (Talanoa/CANLA, 4 Nov) details the impasse over the composition of the Belém indicators taskforce.
  • Mitigation, MWP and TAFF. The TAFF roadmap was launched on 3 November (confirmed by OC, Política por Inteiro, 350.org and CEEW). On the Mitigation Work Programme, which expires at this COP (ENB), there are three positions: extension to 2030 (CAN-I, EU), continuation only if "significantly strengthened" (WWF), and a "nationally determined" facilitative mandate (Presidency). CEEW notes that Santa Marta (57 countries) does not include China or India.
  • Electrification 35 by 35. The "clean/renewable" qualifier is the battleground: EU (Carbon Pulse, 3 Nov), CAN-I, Oil Change, DCJ, CVF ("must be linked to renewable energy generation"), NewClimate/CAT ("35% should be seen as a floor"; current policies deliver 28% in 2035) and CEEW (differentiation; India near 27%) on one side; ICC and We Mean Business prioritise "implementation capacity" over a target. WMB (3 Nov, read in full) asks the presidency to make the "electrification implementation gap" the test of the COP, with a statement from more than 180 companies (US$ 1.69 tn in revenue) and the finding that 69% of executives say they are electrifying faster than their governments are preparing; Mendiluce: "Electrification has momentum, but implementation is lagging." DCJ and the Arab Group reject "parachuting" the target into the cover decision, which makes the migration of the Action Agenda into the negotiated text (foreseen by CSE) more contested.
  • Just transition and BAM. The most united front in civil society: ITUC ("the big win that UNFCCC climate policy urgently needs", with a leadership role for the ILO), CAN-I, CAN Europe (modalities and work schedule for 2027), DCJ (operational until COP32), CEEW and WWF call for structure, governance and resource mobilisation in Antalya. The private sector (ICC, WMB) is silent on the mechanism. The Just Transition Pavilion (ITUC, ILO, DG EMPL, IOE) runs from 9 to 20 November.
  • Loss and damage. Nepal is the test for the FRLD: US$ 21.6 million set aside at the extraordinary meeting of 22 October (NRDC, 350.org), against an estimated reconstruction cost of US$ 4–5 bn (Chatham House); pledges above US$ 800 million, a first replenishment in 2027, and a fund that "could run dry by 2027" (350.org). The V20 calls for a "rules-based assessment framework" for contributions; the L&D Collaboration published key messages (2 Nov) and will maintain "Daily Policy Updates" during the COP.
  • Science and overshoot. The Emissions Gap Report 2026 ("The point of return", 21 Oct) sets the framing: the chance of 1.5 °C without overshoot "is now gone"; cuts of 18%, 45% and 69% by 2030, 2035 and 2040 (vs 2025); 2.8 °C under current policies. Kurum has already incorporated overshoot into official rhetoric; the CVF "refuses to meekly accept" it and plans its own summit; DCJ rejects CDR and geoengineering as a response. After the failure of IPCC-65, an extraordinary session in December will decide whether AR7 arrives in time for GST2.
  • Trade and CBAM. It has gained concreteness: CEEW proposes a permanent technical committee with a mandate at SB66 (Indian aluminium exports to the EU fell by around 42%); the AGN has tabled a request for an agenda item; ICC calls for "full interoperability in carbon border measures"; the Arab Group cites the balance of "US$ 141 bn versus US$ 161 bn" in gains and losses.
  • Cover decision. ENB, Carbon Pulse ("gavel fights") and Stiell ("no big-ticket outcomes", July) reinforce the expectation of a text authored by the presidencies; the dispute is whether electrification and BRIDGE enter it, and with which qualifiers.

Presidency's Action Agenda

The Action Agenda is the voluntary track, running in parallel with the negotiations, and is where Türkiye concentrates its brand. Presented in June and detailed in Kurum's third letter to the Parties (28 August 2026; there are three numbered letters: 13 April, 20 May jointly with Bowen, and 28 August), it has ten priorities: zero waste, oceans and seas, food security, resilient cities, Climate Implementation Bridge, youth and education, green industrialisation, clean energy transition, Rio synergy, and resilient health systems. The letter sets global targets for 2035, "neither prescriptive nor intended to create new obligations": electricity at 35% of final consumption (today around 23%), a reduction of at least 50% in projected growth of municipal solid waste, a drop of at least 25% in building energy intensity, circular materials at at least 15% (today 6.9%), climate education for all and expansion of BRIDGE; the priorities page on cop31.tr adds resilient agriculture. Three pieces deserve special attention.

Electrification "35 by 35". A voluntary target to raise electricity's share of global final consumption from around 23% (baseline in Kurum's letter; other sources use "just over 20%" or 24%) to 35% by 2035, launched by Kurum in Bonn and backed by a strategic partnership with the IEA. Bowen frames it as energy security: the answer to reliability and sovereignty is the same as the one to emissions reduction. The criticism, from Ember to Greenpeace Türkiye, is that the target does not guarantee the new generation is clean: connecting electric vehicles and heat pumps to a grid with 34% coal merely shifts emissions. E3G argues that supporters of the pledge should explain how it unlocks renewables, grids, storage, efficiency, No New Coal and methane, and how it will be financed. Bayraktar is expected to announce Türkiye's updated electrification and renewables targets during the summit (the country aims for 120 GW of solar and wind by 2035, with 90,500 km of lines and a 40 GW HVDC corridor).

Climate Implementation Bridge (BRIDGE). Flagship initiative to turn NDCs and NAPs into investable project portfolios through matchmaking, coordination and technical assistance, with UNDP as design and delivery partner (via "Climate Promise: Forward"). Five pilot countries: Ethiopia, Fiji, Indonesia, Pakistan and Uzbekistan. It is not a new fund and sits outside the negotiated finance agenda. E3G sees value if governance and partners are clear and if the focus is clean energy, grids and storage aligned with national priorities; civil society fears more fragmentation of an already confusing architecture. The test is whether BRIDGE connects to country platforms, the Global Energy Transition Forum and the Global Clean Power Alliance rather than duplicating them.

Green industrialisation and trade. The presidency wants industrial decarbonisation hubs, market creation for low-carbon products, and scale in steel, cement, chemicals, aluminium and fertilisers. The EBRD leads Türkiye's Industrial Decarbonisation Investment Platform (TIDIP, €5 bn by 2030), aimed precisely at the sectors exposed to the European CBAM. TOBB is the "Business Envoy" and organises the Business and Investment Summit on 12–13 November.

Other relevant partnerships: OECD (analysis and dialogues on NDCs, networks, zero waste), AFD (€600 million for the Sea of Marmara mucilage), FAO (Turquoise Nexus Initiative on water, food and adaptation), UNEP/GlobalABC (buildings and cooling pavilion), ICLEI and UCLG (the mayor of Konya, Uğur İbrahim Altay, is special envoy for local governments). A letter from 105 countries calls on COP31 to place the ocean at the centre of climate action.

Who wants what: synthesis by actor

Carbon Brief has analysed around 100 submissions and speeches and keeps an interactive table updated throughout the COP (342 positions as of 4 November, from "priority" to "opposes"). The summary below condenses that database, with complements from E3G and the Heinrich Böll Stiftung infobook marked in italics; the full table, in English, is in the table above.

Three dividing lines stand out clearly in the data: (1) Article 9.1 and burden-sharing: the G77, LMDCs, the Arab Group, AILAC and the Philippines prioritise it; the EU, the UK, Japan, Norway, New Zealand and the EIG oppose it, and the LDCs part ways with the G77 by not supporting burden-sharing; (2) MWP: the EU, the UK, Japan and Norway want continuation to 2030 as a priority, the LMDCs and the Arab Group do not, and the AGN accepts continuation provided no new targets are added; (3) fossil fuels and CBAM: the EU and the UK prioritise a phase-out, Brazil, AILAC and the EIG support it, the Arab Group and Russia do not; Brazil, China, the LMDCs, the Arab Group and Russia oppose the CBAM. The only broad consensus is on oceans. A 350.org report from October ("Partners in Coal") criticises the silence of the two co-hosts on their own coal trade.
sections.brasil:
Brazil in Antalya

Brazil arrives as the outgoing presidency, with four deliverables to report and a clear interest in ensuring that Antalya does not let the Belém legacy dissolve.

  • TAFF Roadmap. Launched on 3 November at the UN House in Brasília by Corrêa do Lago, Ana Toni, João Paulo Capobianco (Minister of the Environment since April 2026) and Marina Silva (now an elected federal deputy, holding no executive post), following the Santa Marta Conference (Colombia and the Netherlands, April 2026, 57 countries). The methodology uses 'archetypes' across three pillars (energy demand, energy supply and macroeconomic resilience), with indicators of exposure and transition capacity that place Parties in four quadrants (structurally vulnerable, constrained, exposed but capable, prepared), without classifying countries by name. The 182-page document proposes a three-stage timetable to 2033: national transition plans by 2028 (in time for the GST2), clean energy expansion in 2029–30 and fossil production cuts from 2030 (a linked piece says 'from 2031' for oil and gas; check the original before quoting). It is voluntary and runs outside the negotiated agenda: it will be presented again at COP31, but the expectation (Política por Inteiro) is that little or nothing will enter the cover decision; the natural destination is to feed the GST2. The second meeting is scheduled for Tuvalu in July 2027, co-hosted by Ireland and Tuvalu. Brazil has not signalled guidelines for a national roadmap of its own; Capobianco is expected to take the topic to Lula later this year. E3G argues for a continuity process that supports national roadmaps as tools for economic transformation; the strategic opportunity is to link TAFF, electrification and implementation finance into a single package. Natalie Unterstell (Talanoa) sums up the success test: a fall in fossil dependence, not the number of plans.
  • Deforestation and TFFF roadmap. The roadmap to end and reverse deforestation and degradation by 2030 combines financial mechanisms, a bioeconomy at scale and command-and-control; Taciana Stec (Talanoa) considers it complete but too focused on national implementation and dependent on adoption by other governments to become an international framework. The Tropical Forest Forever Facility needs US$ 10 billion to begin operating; Norway has pledged US$ 3 billion conditional on reaching that floor by the end of 2026, and the Netherlands US$ 500 million over ten years, while about R$ 2.2 billion was still missing at the end of October. At least 20% of payments go directly to Indigenous peoples and traditional communities. The thematic day on Nature, Land Use and Rio Synergy (17 November) is the natural moment for new pledges.
  • Baku–Belém Roadmap. The presidency is expected to report progress on the roadmap to US$ 1.3 trillion; reducing the cost of capital is one of five areas of action. The Xingu Finance Talks addressed fiscal space for indebted countries; the reform of the IMF and World Bank debt sustainability framework already recognises climate risk and the value of adaptation. The Finance and Trade Day (13 November) and the Leaders' Summit are the windows to signal support for the UK's G20 agenda on debt, MDBs and pre-arranged finance.
  • GIA and Belém Mission to 1.5. The presidencies (COP29, COP30 and COP31) are reporting on the Global Implementation Accelerator; the BM1.5 findings on what is blocking the implementation of NDCs and NAPs are due to be published before Antalya. E3G's test: these initiatives are only worth something if they add demonstrable value to the existing system.
  • Domestic credibility. Brazil is close to its 2025 NDC target (1,320 MtCO₂e): SEEG estimates 1,405.5 MtCO₂e for 2025, about 6.5% above, with the decline driven by deforestation control (the Amazon and the Cerrado at the lowest levels of the PRODES series: 3,335 km² and 5,517 km²). Agriculture (626.3 Mt) and energy (426.8 Mt) remain the largest sources. Lula was re-elected in October; the 2027 draft budget (PLOA) envisages 41% of the Climate Fund financed by oil revenues, and an update of the National Climate Change Policy (PNMC) is on the agenda for year-end.

At the negotiating table, Brazil is part of the coalition seeking continuation of the MWP and has a direct interest in the link between the BAM and the JTWP, in the 59 indicators and in the B2A task force. André Corrêa do Lago represents institutional continuity between Belém and Antalya and personally announced the two roadmaps.

The 'two-level' model that E3G attributes to the Brazilian approach (negotiation provides legitimacy, implementation provides proof) is the most useful framing for defending this legacy in Antalya: the question to ask of each initiative is whether it returns evidence to the formal process or merely adds another acronym.

sections.terreno:
On the ground in Antalya

Venue. Antalya EXPO Fairgrounds, Solak Mahallesi, 07119 Aksu, Antalya. It lies outside the centre: Lara Beach is 16 km away, Kaleiçi (historic centre) 22 km, Konyaaltı 28 km. The ancient city of Perge is 5 km away, for a short break.

Transport. Free buses run through the city during the conference, according to the UNFCCC's official guidance to participants. The airport, the centre and the conference area are linked by the Antray light rail; taxis and public transport are plentiful.

Climate. Mediterranean: daytime highs of 20–21 °C, nighttime lows of 10–11 °C, plenty of sun and occasional rain. Bring an extra layer for the evenings and for air-conditioned rooms.

Customs. Official interactions are warm but formal: use professional titles. Respect for age and hierarchy weighs in meetings. Hospitality is a point of national pride; expect to be served tea at every meeting. Try şiş köfte with Antalya piyaz and the local aubergine dessert (patlıcan reçeli).

Local political context. The elected mayor, Muhittin Böcek (CHP), has been in detention since July 2025 in a corruption investigation, part of a series of cases against the opposition; the acting mayor is Büşra Dirgen Özdemir (CHP). Civic space in the country has been narrowing (Türkiye ranked 163rd of 180 in the 2026 press freedom index), which makes the COP a contested showcase for local activists. Antalya faces water scarcity, microplastics from imported waste from Europe, and a high risk of forest fires in the Taurus mountains; the city council is due to present a Water Action Plan and a Heat Island and Extreme Heat Plan during the COP, with support from UNEP and the UN Chief Heat Officer, Eleni Myrivili.

Operational (E3G checklist). Check visa exemption, accreditation, accommodation and travel; join the intelligence and logistics groups; align talking points and the communications package; identify Brazilian contacts and other critical interlocutors before arriving.

This notice explains how the data of COP31 Navigator newsletter subscribers is handled. The rest of the site requires no registration, uses no cookies and collects no personal data; content from X and YouTube only loads when you ask for it.

What data

Required: your email. Optional: name, organization, country, role and language of the issues. We also record the newsletters you chose and your consent: date and time of subscription and confirmation, the version of this notice and the section of the site where you subscribed.

For what purpose and on what legal basis

To send the issues you chose, in the language you chose, and for aggregate statistics about the audience (for example, how many subscribers per country or role). The legal basis is your consent (LGPD, art. 7, I; GDPR, art. 6(1)(a)), which you can withdraw at any time.

What we do not do

We do not sell or rent data. We do not share the subscriber list with partner organizations, funders or other third parties. We do not use the data for other purposes without asking for new, separate consent. We do not send substantive political analysis without editorial approval.

Who processes the data on our behalf

The email provider stores the list and sends the issues on our behalf, under a data processing agreement. If it is located outside Brazil and the European Economic Area, the international transfer relies on standard contractual clauses (LGPD, art. 33; GDPR, art. 46). The site is hosted on GitHub Pages, which does not receive the form data: it goes straight from your browser to the email provider.

Measurement

We measure subscriptions, confirmations, unsubscribes and delivery failures, always in aggregate. Individual open and click tracking is switched off.

For how long

For as long as the subscription is active. Unconfirmed subscriptions are deleted within 30 days. After you unsubscribe, your email is deleted, or kept only on a suppression list where this is necessary to make sure you do not receive further mailings. Final retention periods: to be confirmed.

Your rights

You can ask for access to, correction, export or deletion of your data, and withdraw your consent, through the contact above or the management link in every issue. You can also lodge a complaint with Brazil's National Data Protection Authority (ANPD) or with the data protection authority in your country.

Security

No subscriber data is stored on this site, in the public repository or in the public data files. The provider's credentials are kept only in protected configuration, outside the code.
